e-9374.problem:
The mass $M(t),$ in grams, of a sample of iron-60 is given by

$$
M(t) = 100 e^{-kt},
$$

where $t$ is the time, in millions of years. The half-life of iron-60 is $2.6$ million years. Rounded to three significant figures, what is the value of $k?$
e-9374.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.
$$

Since we know that $t_{1/2} = 2.6$ million years, we have

$$
2.6 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{2.6} \approx 0.267.
$$

e-6675.problem: The half-life of bismuth-210 is $5.012$ days. How long does it take for a $1\,280\,\textrm g$ sample of bismuth-210 to reduce to $5\,\textrm g?$
e-6675.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that $t_{1/2} = 5.012$ days we have

$$
5.012 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{5.012}
$$

Also, since $M_0 = 1\,280\,\textrm g,$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t) = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
5 = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =1\,280{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \frac{5}{1\,280} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \frac{1}{256} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{256}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/5.012}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡256 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.012} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡256 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{5.012} \\ t & =\frac{5.012\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡256}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈40.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $40$ days for the mass of the substance to reduce to $5\,\textrm g.$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{5\,\text{g}}{1\,280\,\text{g}} \\  & =\frac{1}{256} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{8},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t) =  \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^8\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $8$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $1\,280\,\textrm g$ to $5\,\textrm g.$ Hence,

$$
t = 8\cdot t_{1/2} =8 \cdot 5.012 \approx 40.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $40$ days for the mass of the substance to reduce to $5\,\textrm g.$

e-9373.problem: At a geological site, an object is found with $65\%$ of its original chlorine-36 content. Given that the half-life of chlorine-36 is $301$ thousand years, approximately how old is the object?
e-9373.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.
$$

Since we know that $t_{1/2} = 301$ thousand years, we have

$$
301 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{301}.
$$

So, we have

$$
M(t) = M_0 e^{-t\ln 2/301}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t) = 0.65 M_0.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
0.65M_0 = M_0 e^{-t\ln 2/301}
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}0.65{M}_{0} & ={M}_{0}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301} \\ 0.65\cancel{{M}_{0}} & =\cancel{{M}_{0}}{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301} \\ 0.65 & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.65) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/301}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.65) & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{301} \\ t & =-\frac{301\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.65)}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & ≈187.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the object is approximately $187$ thousand years old.

M(t)=8e−0.02567t,

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
The mass $M(t),$ in micrograms, of a sample of curium-240 is given by

$$
M(t)=8{e}^{-0.025\,67t},
$$

where $t$ is the time, in days. Rounded to one decimal place, what is the half-life of curium-240?
after.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

We're given that $k=0.025\,67.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1/2} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{0.025\,67} \\  & ≈27.0\,\text{days}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The mass $M(t)$ of a radioactive substance at time $t$ can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
{M}^{′}(t)=-kM(t),\,M(0)={M}_{0}.
$$

The general solution to this equation is

$$
M(t)={M}_{0}{e}^{-kt}.
$$

The half-life ${t}_{1/2}$ is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

$$
{t}_{1/2}=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}.
$$

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

**Method 1**

Since we know that ${t}_{1/2}=50\,\text{s},$ we have

$$
50=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{k}\,⇒\,k=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{50}
$$

Also, since ${M}_{0}=400\,\mu \text{g},$ we have the particular solution

$$
M(t)=400{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50}.
$$

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=50\,\mu \text{g}.$ So, we set up our equation as follows:

$$
50=400{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50}\,\,
$$

Solving this equation for $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}50 & =400{e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50} \\ \frac{50}{400} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50} \\ \frac{1}{8} & ={e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-t\operatorname{ln}⁡2/50}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{50} \\ -\operatorname{ln}⁡8 & =-\frac{t\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{50} \\ t & =\frac{50\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡8}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ t & =150.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes $150\,\text{s}$ for the mass of the substance to reduce to $50\,\mu \text{g}.$

**Method 2**

We wish to calculate the time $t$ such that $M(t)=50\,\mu \text{g}.$ Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{M(t)}{M(0)} & =\frac{50\,\mu \text{g}}{400\,\mu \text{g}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

or equivalently

$$
M(t)={(\frac{1}{2})}^{3}\cdot M(0).
$$

From this equation, we see that $3$ half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from $400\,\mu \text{g}$ to $50\,\mu \text{g}.$ Hence,

$$
t=3\cdot {t}_{1/2}=3\cdot 50\,\text{s}=150\,\text{s}.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that it takes $150\,\text{s}$ for the mass of the substance to reduce to $50\,\mu \text{g}.$

t1/2=ln⁡2k.

50=ln⁡2k⇒k=ln⁡250

Also, since M0=400μg, we have the particular solution

M(t)=400e−tln⁡2/50.

We wish to calculate the time t such that M(t)=50μg. So, we set up our equation as follows:

M(t)M(0)=50μg400μg=18=(12)3,

or equivalently

M(t)=(12)3⋅M(0).

From this equation, we see that 3 half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from 400μg to 50μg. Hence,

At an archaeological site, an object is found with 30% of its original carbon-14 content. Given that the half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years, approximately how old is the object?

9827 years

The mass M(t) of a radioactive substance at time t can be modeled by the differential equation

M′(t)=−kM(t),M(0)=M0.

The general solution to this equation is

M(t)=M0e−kt.

The half-life t1/2 is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

t1/2=ln⁡2k.

Since we know that t1/2=5730 years, we have

5730=ln⁡2k⇒k=ln⁡25730.

So, we have M(t)=M0e−tln⁡2/5730.

We wish to calculate the time t such that M(t)=0.3M0. So, we set up our equation as follows:

0.3M0=M0e−tln⁡2/5730

Solving this equation for t, we get

0.3M0=M0e−tln⁡2/57300.3M0=M0e−tln⁡2/57300.3=e−tln⁡2/5730ln⁡(0.3)=ln⁡(e−tln⁡2/5730)ln⁡(0.3)=−tln⁡25730t=−5730⋅ln⁡(0.3)ln⁡2t≈9953

Therefore, we conclude that the object is approximately 9953 years old.
